sections.html: Tometes kranponhah grows to around 40 cm in length. As an adult it has a black spot on the gill cover.

The Rio Xingu is a clear water tributary of the Amazon in Brazil. Two new Tometes species were described from the rapids area in 2016, namely T. kranponhah and T. anclorhynchus. Tometes kranponhah is an endemic of the Xingu, where it is said to be quite common. In contrast, there are only a few collections of T. anclorhynchus, but that species is more widespread and also occurs in the system of the Rio Tocantins.
Little can be said about the behaviour. Juveniles (10 specimens, 5–7 cm long) were somewhat quarrelsome among themselves, as shown by slight fin damage, but this was kept within acceptable limits.

It has turned out that the animals originally offered were Mylesinus paucisquamatus from the Rio Tocantins, and the statement that they came from the Rio Xingu was a mistake.

New species of large fish are still being found in the rivers of South America, mainly because many species look extraordinarily similar. For some, such as the large silver dollars or pacus, there is also the fact that they undergo quite dramatic changes in shape and colour during their lives (ontogenetic changes).

The two Tometes species look quite similar. The main distinguishing feature is the mouth shape. T. kranponhah has a black spot on the gill cover as an adult, which is missing in T. anclorhynchus. They also differ in final size: T. kranponhah grows to around 40 cm, while T. anclorhynchus reaches around 30 cm.
